 1    Introduction
Predicting the next symbol of a dependent process differs from estimating its transition table
uniformly. The query is the terminal context of the same trajectory used for estimation. A
context that appears only near the end can be statistically important even though it has few earlier
departures. Adversarial replacement of recorded symbols adds a second difficulty: a changed symbol
alters several overlapping triples and can change which observations appear to belong to the queried
row.
    This paper studies these effects without an intermediate information bottleneck. The predictor
receives every corrupted symbol and may perform arbitrary computation. Corruption happens
before any encoding. Thus the lower bounds cannot be removed by storing more of the corrupted
input or by improving an internal representation. Conversely, the upper rules use counts directly;
their performance does not rely on a restricted neural architecture.
    The principal distinction is between protecting and not protecting the terminal pair. With
protection, a logarithmic accumulation of rare informative suffixes determines the corruption price.
Binary sources have a different cutoff from sources with three or more symbols. Without protection,
even a known first-order source can leave irreducible uncertainty about the true final symbol after
one erasure. The latter is uncertainty about the prediction target itself, not merely about estimating
an unknown transition probability.

Relation to earlier work. Prediction from a Markov trajectory, and lower bounds based on
a common prior and waiting-time structure, have established precedents; see Han, Jana and Wu
[3]. We do not claim that those general ideas originate here. Robust Markov inference also has a
substantial existing literature. Ghosh [2] studies parametric inference for stationary ergodic finite
chains, including contamination of the transition matrix by rowwise mixtures. That contamination
acts on the transition law, rather than replacing a fixed number of entries in a realized word.
Zuckerman [5] studies robustness of Markov dynamics; its abstract concerns limiting frequencies
and mixing, hitting and cover times for reversible chains. Bhatt et al. [1] study contaminated mean
estimation under moment assumptions. These comparisons distinguish the declared experiments,
not establish priority for the present rates. Our reading of Ghosh covers the abstract, introduction
and Section 2.3; our comparisons with Zuckerman and Bhatt et al. are abstract-level only. The
transport-coupling work of O’Connor, McGoff and Nobel [4] was screened at abstract level for
long-run stationary transition couplings, not audited as a source of the finite bridge theorem proved
here.

Proof organization and dependency boundary. We first state the experiment, rates and
statistical-order budget consequence. The technical sections give the new perturbation, erasure,
binary transport and endpoint arguments in full. They import a clean actual-terminal add-one
bound from the predecessor dossier (R011), a stationary clipped-occupation inequality (IU001),
and binary weighted-occupation interfaces (BIF001 and BAI003 version 2). The arbitrary-start
residual decomposition is given explicitly, following AU001. These inherited interfaces are stated
with their domains at the point of use. Their full original proofs and reviews remain in the
accompanying predecessor dossier, whose exact paths and hashes are listed in the source manifest.
This manuscript is therefore not a claim to newly rederive the entire foundational clean-prediction
chain. The preserved companion manuscript on finite information cuts addresses different, internal
representation restrictions.

4    Scope of the synthesis
The protected upper and lower directions have different mechanisms. For K ≥ 3, direct histogram
stability is combined with terminal occupation, while exact exchangeability erases the active suffix
arrangement. For binary sources, a pessimistic designated-exit estimator exploits a weighted
occupation inequality. Its lower witness has variable-length cycles, so a cheap modification with the
wrong output marginal is not enough. Entropy transport supplies a weaker bridge approximation,
and a finite scalar argument shows that its genuine horizon cutoff does not change the final order.
    The binary lower is an existence result for a common stochastic map assembled from finite
rational transport tables. It makes no efficient sampling claim. The upper count rule has a
straightforward finite rational description, but no assertion about a Transformer’s bounded depth,
width, attention budget, training dynamics or learnability follows. These resources require separate
theorems with the same input and fault permissions. Likewise, offline history-adaptive kernels,
causal corruption and visible-mask models are not interchangeable here.

 1    Introduction
Predicting the next symbol of a dependent process differs from estimating its transition table
uniformly. The query is the terminal context of the same trajectory used for estimation. A
context that appears only near the end can be statistically important even though it has few earlier
departures. Adversarial replacement of recorded symbols adds a second difficulty: a changed symbol
alters several overlapping triples and can change which observations appear to belong to the queried
row.
    This paper studies these effects without an intermediate information bottleneck. The predictor
receives every corrupted symbol and may perform arbitrary computation. Corruption happens
before any encoding. Thus the lower bounds cannot be removed by storing more of the corrupted
input or by improving an internal representation. Conversely, the upper rules use counts directly;
their performance does not rely on a restricted neural architecture.
    The principal distinction is between protecting and not protecting the terminal pair. With
protection, a logarithmic accumulation of rare informative suffixes determines the corruption price.
Binary sources have a different cutoff from sources with three or more symbols. Without protection,
even a known first-order source can leave irreducible uncertainty about the true final symbol after
one erasure. The latter is uncertainty about the prediction target itself, not merely about estimating
an unknown transition probability.

Relation to earlier work. Prediction from a Markov trajectory, and lower bounds based on
a common prior and waiting-time structure, have established precedents; see Han, Jana and Wu
[3]. We do not claim that those general ideas originate here. Robust Markov inference also has a
substantial existing literature. Ghosh [2] studies parametric inference for stationary ergodic finite
chains, including contamination of the transition matrix by rowwise mixtures. That contamination
acts on the transition law, rather than replacing a fixed number of entries in a realized word.
Zuckerman [5] studies robustness of Markov dynamics; its abstract concerns limiting frequencies
and mixing, hitting and cover times for reversible chains. Bhatt et al. [1] study contaminated mean
estimation under moment assumptions. These comparisons distinguish the declared experiments,
not establish priority for the present rates. Our reading of Ghosh covers the abstract, introduction
and Section 2.3; our comparisons with Zuckerman and Bhatt et al. are abstract-level only. The
transport-coupling work of O’Connor, McGoff and Nobel [4] was screened at abstract level for
long-run stationary transition couplings, not audited as a source of the finite bridge theorem proved
here.

Proof organization and dependency boundary. We first state the experiment, rates and
statistical-order budget consequence. The technical sections give the new perturbation, erasure,

This manuscript is therefore not a claim to newly rederive the entire foundational clean-prediction

4    Scope of the synthesis
The protected upper and lower directions have different mechanisms. For K ≥ 3, direct histogram
stability is combined with terminal occupation, while exact exchangeability erases the active suffix
arrangement. For binary sources, a pessimistic designated-exit estimator exploits a weighted
occupation inequality. Its lower witness has variable-length cycles, so a cheap modification with the
wrong output marginal is not enough. Entropy transport supplies a weaker bridge approximation,
and a finite scalar argument shows that its genuine horizon cutoff does not change the final order.
    The binary lower is an existence result for a common stochastic map assembled from finite
rational transport tables. It makes no efficient sampling claim. The upper count rule has a
straightforward finite rational description, but no assertion about a Transformer’s bounded depth,
width, attention budget, training dynamics or learnability follows. These resources require separate
theorems with the same input and fault permissions. Likewise, offline history-adaptive kernels,
causal corruption and visible-mask models are not interchangeable here.
    The technical proofs below imply Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 by taking maxima of the separately
established lower floors and using the stated upper rules. All genuinely new ingredients are included;
the explicitly named inherited interfaces retain their original evidence status. Independent LLM
reviews and finite diagnostics in the dossier are corroborating mathematical checks, not formal
